content: An aphthous ulcer, commonly referred to as a canker sore, is a type of painful open sore that occurs inside the mouth due to a disruption in the mucous membrane. This condition is also known as aphthous stomatitis and, in cases of multiple or recurring ulcers, may be referred to as Sutton's Disease. Aphthous ulcers are classified into three categories: major aphthous stomatitis, minor aphthous stomatitis, and herpetiform stomatitis. The exact pathophysiology of aphthous ulcers remains unclear. The development of recurrent aphthous ulcers is thought to vary depending on underlying medical conditions. Proposed mechanisms include the cross-reactivity theory involving microbial antigens and mitochondrial heat shock proteins, the dysembryoplastic theory, histopathogenesis of glandular cells in myxoma, and the thrombotic theory. Predisposing factors identified so far include trauma, cessation of smoking, stress, hormonal imbalances, and food hypersensitivities. The precise cause of aphthous ulcers is unknown. However, several factors are known to provoke their occurrence, including stress, fatigue, illness, accidental biting injuries, hormonal changes, menstruation, sudden weight loss, food allergies, the foaming agent sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) in toothpaste, and deficiencies in vitamin B12, iron, and folic acid. Aphthous ulcers must be differentiated from other conditions such as malignant ulcers, infections, and systemic diseases like rheumatic or cutaneous disorders. The prevalence of aphthous ulcers is estimated to range from 1,000 to 60,000 cases per 100,000 individuals annually among both adults and children. Common risk factors for recurrent aphthous ulcers include the use of dentures or braces, gender, age, family history, oral diseases, and stress. Routine screening for gonadoblastoma is not recommended in the context of aphthous ulcers. However, patients with XY gonadal abnormalities should undergo sonographic monitoring starting at age 2, every six months, until the gonads are removed. The natural history, complications, and prognosis of recurrent aphthous ulcers vary depending on the severity of the disease. There is no single diagnostic test for aphthous ulcers. Symptoms typically include oral pain, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), and oral bumps that may have resolved spontaneously in the past. On physical examination, patients may present with ulcers that are shallow or deep, small (1–5 in number) or large (5–100 in number), and may or may not result in scarring. These characteristics assist physicians in classifying the disease. There are no specific laboratory, electrocardiographic, X-ray, ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, or other imaging findings associated with aphthous ulcers. Similarly, no other diagnostic studies are specific to this condition. Most cases of aphthous ulcers are self-limiting and require only supportive care. They typically heal without treatment within 1 to 2 weeks. Maintaining good oral hygiene is essential, and avoiding spicy, acidic, and salty foods and drinks is recommended, as these can irritate existing ulcers and exacerbate pain. Strong mouthwashes, such as Listerine, may also cause irritation due to their potent ingredients, and their use is discouraged during active ulcers. Surgical intervention is not recommended for the management of aphthous ulcers. There is no established method for the primary prevention of aphthous ulcers. However, maintaining dental hygiene and attending regular dental check-ups are strongly advised to improve oral health and reduce the risk of developing aphthous ulcers. Similarly, there is no established method for secondary prevention of aphthous ulcers. Nonetheless, good dental hygiene and regular visits to the dentist are highly recommended to promote oral health and minimize the risk of recurrence.
